utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Are you ready to proceed, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mrs. Lopicic. We shall continue where we left off yesterday. If you remember, we were talking about your final opinion in your expert report. And my next question would be related to the following fact. In these proceedings, a large number of witnesses said that Mitar Vasiljevic, consuming alcohol in large quantities, was in a state when he talked a lot, frequently in a disconnected manner but they also said that in that state, he was not aggressive. If that is true, does that correspond to what you established during your examination or is that in contradiction with what you established during the examination?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, and in the course of my interview, I had no information whatsoever and no evidence of any kind of aggressiveness on his part. On the contrary, he himself described himself as a person that was not prone to any outbursts of an aggressive nature. In fact, he said, and I refer to this in my opinion, that he liked to crack jokes, even at his own expense, and also to talk about -- to brag about things that he never did, in order to amuse others. As for what you said, that other people did not see him as an aggressive person, is another piece of information that supports this assumption. One might make a psychiatric assumption as to his aggressiveness, if it is possible to talk about that at all. On the basis of all the findings that have been collected so far, it might be said that his aggressiveness may be auto-aggressiveness, if we interpret his alcoholism as an act of destruction of himself. So I don't see any evidence of any aggressiveness towards others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Domazet, I think we will need some explanation of the second last sentence of that answer. "It might be said that his aggressiveness," of which she says she has found no evidence, "may be auto-aggressiveness." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Lopicic, I hope you understood Judge Hunt's question. So could you please explain what you meant by auto-aggressiveness and aggressiveness towards others? Would you elaborate on that a little?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aggression as a dynamic factor is a component part of the personality. All of us have this instinct for survival and for aggression, and it is still not clearly defined as an instinct but it is something that we do carry, a dynamic, psychodynamic and psychoanalytical interpretation of alcoholism interpreted as an act of auto-aggression or self-aggression. That is why I said this chronic alcoholism of his could be an unconscious act of aggressiveness towards himself. Now, why I am mentioning this as an assumption for consideration? Because we have this evidence of hereditary -- of the hereditary factor, which tell us that his mother and his aunt destroyed themselves, and that is what has prompted me to make these comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So, Mrs. Lopicic, when you refer to auto-aggression, what you mean is that due to excessive consumption of alcohol and by becoming an alcoholic he's destroying himself, and you see that as an act of auto-aggression. Thank you for your answer. My next question is something that you have already answered in part, and it has to do with his aggressiveness towards third persons in view of his mental disease, but as it is important, could you be a little more specific?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information, autoanamnestic information, which would relate to aggressiveness against others, and you yourself told us about what witnesses have said, describing him as a person who was prone to making jokes and amusing others rather than being aggressive toward others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, but my question was whether that corresponds to what you yourself found regarding his condition.

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, she can only rely upon what the accused has said to her. Now, if he has said something to her which contradicts what he has said here in court, it's worth referring to. But I don't think, if I may say so, it assists us at all to have this witness give us an opinion based upon what she has established during the course of her conversation with the accused if all that she has got is what the accused has told her. She can interpret it, but this is just sort of trying to bolster your client's evidence. The fact that he repeated it to the psychiatrist doesn't seem to me to take that very far. So can we get on to matters upon which the doctor can help us on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to verify whether what the witnesses have said - and of course it will be up to Your Honours to judge that evidence - whether it was in any way in contradiction with what Dr. Lopicic established during her interview. But I've done with that, and I will go on to my final question regarding her opinion and that is the question of responsibility, mental responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It emanates from your opinion that Mitar Vasiljevic, while being treated in hospital in Uzice, was completely irresponsible and that in the period covered by the indictment. So could you explain what period you had in mind his accountability was considerably reduced, of course on the basis of the classification we have in Yugoslavia. So could you elaborate on that a little?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The period of hospitalisation and the period of psychosis which was evident from the clinical findings, from the case history, and the anamnestic information we obtained was a period when the patient was unaccountable as he had no orientation. He was disoriented. He was outside reality, as we put it. As I explained yesterday, psychosis is a condition when the patient is out of touch with reality. The period prior to hospitalisation, the so prodromal or introductory period to the psychosis I think can be viewed dynamically, bearing in mind the three factors I spoke about yesterday. And this dynamic relationship with those three factors must not be neglected. So this is something that was of significance at the subjective level for our client. He showed a -- certain signs of unusual behaviour, strange behaviour. That is how he himself describes it, and I heard you mention it here yesterday as well. And what I was told by Dr. Vasiljevic, that in that period - and I think that was at the beginning of June - he was in a condition in which, according to Dr. Vasiljevic, he spoke about demons and angels. He was put in detention because he refused to carry out orders required of him by his superiors. And he told me, with reference to that period, that he was under enormous fear. If we know that fear is a generator of psychopathology and the basis of any psychosis, then it can be said that this was an introduction to his psychosis, and in that condition, we consider the patient to have significantly reduced accountability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think you'll have to try and get the doctor to be a little bit more precise. If he was having fear throughout the whole time that he was working near the front, was he having a psychosis from that alone at that time? It's fairly important in this case, from your client's point of view, Mr. Domazet, that this is defined or this period is defined just a little bit more precisely than simply saying, "Well, these are the things which could have caused it." It may be that the doctor was unable to put a period on it, but simply to say that fear is one of three factors which might bring on this psychosis, and if he suffered fear right back many, many weeks before he went to hospital, then he was suffering from a psychosis from that date doesn't strike me as being very logical. He may be psychiatrically sound, I don't know, but I think you have to try and get the doctor to be a little more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure you understand Judge Hunt, so will you please try and give an answer?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say that fear is a generator of psychopathology, then I mean that the period prior to hospitalisation was the pre-psychotic period, a period in which Mr. Vasiljevic had certain symptoms and a certain psychopathology which was not so manifest for the surroundings as it was for him. To be more specific, he says that in that period he had this urge to blink involuntarily. He was blinking all the time. This can be considered as a symptom whereby he was relieving himself of fear. It's a physiological mechanism, a way in which one relieves oneself of fear quite unconsciously. Something else that was linked to this blinking, this is an automatic act, and this was linked to certain compulsive thinking, in the form of exaggerated ideas. He said if he blinked and it was dark, somebody would get killed or somebody would die. So he attached symbolic, magical significance to this compulsive blinking. If there is light, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Doctor, you told us all of this yesterday. I want, if I can get from you, a very straightforward answer to what I see myself, as a non-psychiatrist, to be a very simple question. If he was suffering prior to his admission, as part of his pre-psychosis period is the expression you used, was he unaccountable, within the meaning of the Yugoslav statute, for his actions? Before he went to hospital. That's what we have to determine. We are not interested in the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my report, I have stated that very clearly. In our legislation, there is a category of significantly reduced accountability, and I think that we cannot put an equation mark between the pre-hospitalisation and the hospitalisation period, because perception, observation, was still preserved. He gave information about that period which are relevant and which are in line with the information we obtained earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But, doctor, does that statement by you, "We cannot put an equation mark between the pre-hospitalisation and the hospitalisation period," mean that he was not suffering from a reduced accountability before he went to hospital? That's what I want to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He did suffer from reduced accountability before hospitalisation, quite clearly. I cannot say that it is the same kind of unaccountability as it was when he was hospitalised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well then, how far was his accountability reduced before he went to hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our legislation, we have this category which is defined as significantly reduced, and reduced. I don't know what you expect me to say. Do you want me to express myself in percentages? But according to our legislation, we have three categories of accountability: reduced accountability, significantly reduced accountability and unaccountability. Those are the three degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well then, when did he become significantly -- when did his accountability become significantly reduced? Was it before he went to hospital? I'm sorry to try to pin you down, but this is the issue which you are here to discuss and what -- and the issue which we have to determine, and it doesn't help, if I may say so, to keep on describing his symptoms. Can you tell us when you say he became -- his accountability became significantly reduced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before he went to prison. This act of imprisonment is a moment when his behaviour significantly changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, we've now got an answer. It's over to you, Mr. Domazet. It's not, if I may say so, entirely a logical one, but it's a matter for you. It's something upon which you bear an onus of proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you well, Dr. Lopicic, on the basis of the information you have prior to hospitalisation, you are of the opinion that from the period prior to his imprisonment in Uzamnica, shortly prior, you consider that period to be one of reduced accountability. As for the period prior to that, you have no such evidence, if I understand you correctly, and that is why your answer is that this is the period immediately prior to his going to prison.

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information I was given, in this opinion, I said that I was given information as of March, 1992. However, what we find in his statement is that it was precisely that period prior to going to prison, that is when the front line was changed and he had to pass through territory that were very risky and he was frightened, so let me not repeat myself. That is something that leads me to believe that his mental condition started to deteriorate then and that that was an introduction to his psychosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: His Honour Judge Hunt asked, if he was fearful at the front, of what was being done at the front, to what extent could that alone have affected the development of the disease. Did you have in mind all the other factors, the biological ones, the chronic alcoholism, or only the stress factor which you also, I think, attributed to the overall situation?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite precise, I must say that observing and interpreting the findings of Mr. Vasiljevic, these three factors are dynamically interconnected throughout his life. It is impossible to exclude the significance of any one of those factors, the hereditary factor, alcoholism and stress. I won't repeat what I said. Living conditions, the acute situations he found himself in, the loss of a close relative, the fracture, all these are stressful events biologically and psychologically, and they certainly have a very important role, and the interplay of those factors is such that it is impossible to determine how much each of those factors contribute to the general situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Finally, you still uphold your opinion that in the period prior to admission to hospital - because this is a significant period for us - his accountability in the legal sense, according to the current legislation in Yugoslavia, was significantly reduced? Finally, since in your report and especially in your oral statement here, you refer to certain documents which you obtained immediately prior to coming to The Hague, and which you referred to yesterday, saying that you would like to give them to the court. You have the originals so could you please hand them over, as we will be hearing the expert opinion of another doctor called by the Prosecution, who has not been able to see these documents, so I hope he will be able to review them before coming to Court, as, regarding the hereditary factor, we heard no prior information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could I ask the usher to take over these documents? I have also distributed copies to the interpreters. And I would like to ask Mrs. Lopicic to comment on these documents. As her report has been admitted under D43, I think that these documents, as a component part of that report, could be D43.1 onwards. The first of those documents is a decision of the municipal court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment. Have you got these, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday when I heard about Mrs. Vasiljevic's death certificate, I asked for a copy of that and received a copy. It's being translated now. I have not received any of the other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I see. Well, then, you better reserve your position about their admissibility until you've heard about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is that the way of dealing with it? You proceed, Mr. Domazet. I think that the -- it would be safer to leave their marking as an exhibit until after we've heard something of them, because Mr. Groome is in a position -- he can't say he objects to them or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do we all have copies? Are they in English or are they in B/C/S? Give us the copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, all these documents were shown to me for the first time here, so they are all in B/C/S, and that is why I have given them to the interpreters for us to be able to understand each one of them more easily. Of course it would be better to have a translation in the meantime. The first three documents relate to the death of Mitar Vasiljevic's mother. One is a decision by the court proclaiming her dead, and the other two are a report from the registry regarding -- producing a death certificate and a marriage certificate as confirmation of the fact that this was his mother. And the others -- the next document is a discharge document with epicrisis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just a moment. Does the decision of the court identify the cause of death? If not, I'm not sure what the relevance of all this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Honour. In the explanation for the decision, it says that on the basis of the statements of witnesses, and I can quote: "It has been established that Vojka Vasiljevic, on the 4th of July, 1963, went in an unknown direction," and they consider that she committed suicide. According to their statements, she was mentally disturbed so that she frequently repeated that one day she would leave and that no one would know anything about her. And so they believe that she most probably jumped into the Drina and died, the Drina River. That is from the explanation of the decision which was issued five years after death. Following the normal legal procedure which was binding according to the law, a notice was issued in the Official Gazette, and after that, the court heard witnesses and proclaimed her dead. And the decision is dated 1969.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other two documents were taken out of the registry quite recently as a death certificate. The fourth document has to do with Stojanka Blagojevic that Dr. Lopicic spoke of. It is the discharge paper from the Uzice hospital from 1984. And all the other documents relate to Mitar Vasiljevic's niece. I would rather not mention her name, because in that case we would need to go into private session. And all the other documents have to do with the treatment of that niece.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then, is the discharge statement relating to the aunt the one -- does that refer to the fact that she drank some sort of poison? Vinegar, yes, very strong vinegar. Is that the one? It's just that we've got to know what these documents are, and Mr. Groome has no opportunity of --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I think it would be best for this discharge document to be read out by Dr. Lopicic as it is in Latin and if she could translate it, the Latin terms for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, please, Doctor. And remember, please speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will. It is the last period in hospital, though we know that she was treated before, but I have no other case histories or discharge documents except this last one from which we see that she was admitted on the 30th of September, 1984 to the general hospital in Uzice, to the psychiatric ward with the diagnosis depressive psychosis, attempted suicide, intoxication with this strong vinegar. And as a consequence of that, her kidneys were affected. And in an attempt to restore them because there was kidney insufficiency, they did laparotomy and peritoneal dialysis. This is an attempt to overcome the problem with means of a dialysis machine. This was not successful and the patient died on the 25th of October, 1984 at 2100 hours at the urology ward where the dialysis was done at the hospital in Titovo Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is that all, Mrs. Lopicic, from this document?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you wish me to translate the description as well? [In English] The patient was accepted to the neuropsychiatry department as an urgent -- as an urgent case because of intoxication of some amount of [Interpretation] [No translation]. [In English] Yes. She was removed to the urology and there was done the lab analysis. Because of the general renal dysfunction, peritoneal dialysis was done. And this was functioning for a few days. It seems that the -- her -- her case was improving. But the last few days it was a [Interpretation] deterioration, deterioration. [In English] Then the esophagoscopy was done as of -- yes. And -- [Interpretation] [No translation]. Yes, I have some problems to translate the -- this sluznica jenjaka [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Don't worry about it, Doctor. We can have the original translated into English by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But it was the Latin, Doctor, that we wanted you to translate, because none of us know the Latin terminology used by doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is actually the only document relating to Mr. Vasiljevic's aunt, and the others relate to his niece. And perhaps Dr. Lopicic could explain what those documents are. But I think there is a danger of identification, so I would prefer us to do that in private session, with your permission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We are back in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Doctor, I'd like to begin by asking you a few more questions about your findings regarding whether or not Mr. Vasiljevic is an aggressive person, and I guess the first question I'd like to ask you is: The fact that other people may believe that a person is non-aggressive when they drink, or is non-aggressive generally, that doesn't mean that that person is incapable of committing a violent act, does it?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is something that is quite significant when we talk about the propensity to aggression. We also have to mention an ability to control these tendencies. All of us have some aggression within us, but within normal limits. When we talk about normal tendencies, that means we should be able to control these tendencies, propensities for aggression. I have no information indicating that Mr. Vasiljevic had -- did not have an ability to control his propensity for aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And it's possible that people who are normal psychologically and can control their aggression, they are in fact capable of committing violent acts if they so choose to do so; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is beyond control, and conditions that can lead to us to lose control can be different, depending on the motive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, I'm just -- let's take the most basic case of somebody with no history of mental disease, whose friends and family agree that they are not aggressive, they are not aggressive whether they are sober and they are not aggressive when they are drunk. You would agree with me that that person is capable of one day deciding to kill another person and then in fact kill that person? You would agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all of us have different capabilities within us. This is a hypothetical situation that we are discussing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. So the fact that somebody says that somebody is not aggressive isn't evidence that they are incapable of committing a violent act; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we have to discuss absolute evidence and relative ones. If you wish to put this in the sphere of relative evidence, then you are right, but if we are to trust the person making the statement, then it will be different. The more information there is that is -- that corresponds or that goes together well in the description of one's personality, then that is further evidence that that is a correct description.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. That brings me to -- something else I want to ask you is, you have done some work here to try to corroborate some of the things that you were told, and I commend you for that, but will you agree with me that primarily your findings are based upon information that was provided to you and you accepting that information as true, and then rendering your opinion based on that information that you were provided; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mostly relied on my own findings. In this case, I relied on a finding made by me during an interview I had with Mr. Vasiljevic in the detention unit on the 23rd and 24th of November. I didn't know him prior to that, and I had no information on him except for the medical documentation I was given prior to coming here. Information I received from others, if you have in mind Dr. Vasiljevic and Dr. Simic, those are the only two medical professionals I had an opportunity to meet and consult, and the information given to me by them was just something I used to verify some presumptions and some details that I obtained based on my interview with Mr. Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let's take the example of Dr. Vasiljevic. Isn't it a fact that you used information from Dr. Vasiljevic to come to a rather significant conclusion about his relative, Mr. Vasiljevic here in court? It wasn't simply to verify but it was -- you drew some rather significant conclusions based on what Dr. Vasiljevic told you happened in the beginning of June? Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My conclusion -- my presumption, rather, because conclusion is something that is given at the end after all the information has been processed, my presumption at that time, since I processed some relevant information about his psychosis, every clinical specialist that follows patients has to assume that there is a period during which when a patient experiences some subjective disturbances can be visible only to a psychiatrist or somebody who is an expert. What I obtained from Dr. Vasiljevic simply confirmed the assumption that I obtained through anamnesis of the patient indicating that he had certain disturbances during that period. So what Dr. Vasiljevic told me was not a decisive factor in creating my opinion that -- my conclusion that this was a pre-psychotic period. This simply confirmed my thoughts or my thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In response to, I believe, a question from the bench regarding when you believed this psychotic disturbance began, you use as evidence of when it began your conversation with Dr. Vasiljevic, who told you, in the beginning of June of 1992, he began to talk about certain things, and it was that conversation with Dr. Vasiljevic which you cited as evidence of when his mental condition deteriorated; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat that this simply confirmed my assumption that I obtained through the findings, and I will quote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Doctor, you've quoted it before. Mr. Groome, I think you can accept that she really is relying upon it as evidence. It may not be initial evidence, but it is evidence, so you can proceed on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Doctor, is there any other evidence, aside from what Dr. Vasiljevic told you, that you used to fix a date as to when you believed Mr. Vasiljevic -- his accountability was severely [sic] reduced?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is that period prior to his arrest or, rather, the mere reason of arrest. To me, as someone who views the patient in that condition and in that period of time is further proof that something was wrong with him. Not only because of the fear that he said he had suffered but also due to a very relevant fact that when somebody in the time of war refuses to carry out an order risks being held accountable under martial law. So he was not critical with respect to the risk in which he found himself. He refused to carry out an order. And only a person who has not -- no knowledge of the consequences that would follow could do something like this, like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, just one moment. I'm sorry, it may have been wrongly typed, but your question was that she had fixed a date as to when his accountability was severely reduced. She used the word "significantly," as I understand it, which is not quite the same as "severely."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think it's -- I probably misspoke, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But the terminology from the statute to which the doctor referred was "significantly."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "Significantly," yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Doctor, let me ask you a hypothetical question. If I were to come to you for treatment and express some concerns about my mental condition, and I said to you I felt fine, I've had no sense that I have anything wrong with me mentally up until about six months ago when my mother tragically died, and ever since then I've been suffering from -- and I give you the symptoms I'm suffering from and my belief that I have a psychological problem, would you use that information to help you determine that probably the tragic event of my mother's loss was the starting point of my mental difficulties?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] If you want, we can discuss hypothetically, but first I want to ask you -- [Interpretation] Pardon me. If we were to discuss hypothetically, then my first question would be -- my first question to you would be: "Why did you come?" When somebody comes to a psychiatrist, that person has to have a reason behind it. The mere fact that a person came to see a psychiatrist has a certain significance. If in the anamnesis we receive the information that you indicated, then we have to take it into account. We have to analyse that information. We cannot ignore it. We cannot say somebody is feeling well now but something happened in their childhood, they'd lost a parent, or ignore this. I did not say -- I did not discuss yesterday the simple fact of a loss. I mentioned an example of a two-month old baby who had lost a mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What I'm getting at, and I want to see if you'll agree with me, that my own perception of what it was that caused me to have difficulty is an important fact, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And if I were to tell you that prior to my mother's death I have -- I've had no psychological problems and there's no evidence to suggest otherwise, would a doctor such as yourself presume that the person was in good mental health prior to the mother's death?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would always look into that. We have to take that into an account -- into account because it's a factor of risk. It doesn't mean that it was a provocative factor in that particular situation, but it's a certain risk that we have to keep in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, doctor, you spoke to Mr. Vasiljevic about two different crimes that he's been charged with. Did you ask Mr. Vasiljevic during your interview, "Mr. Vasiljevic, what do you think your mental state was at the time those men were killed at the river?" Did you ask him that question?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask him that question when we discussed that event. I asked him that question much before that when we discussed alcoholism. What is evident is that Mr. Vasiljevic did not realise that he was an alcoholic, nor did he realise that he had mental problems. I asked him whether in May or beginning of June, when he started blinking, whether -- and when he had certain thoughts whether at that time he was aware that some -- that he was going through a certain situation. He told me that he only realised that that was fear at the time, and he didn't think further about it. He didn't know if it was a mental problem or something from God at the time. He simply was not aware of his mental condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Doctor, over a year ago, Mr. Vasiljevic was interviewed over the course of two days in great detail about the events which you also discussed with him, and he was asked a specific question regarding his own perception of his mental health. I'm going to read his answer to you, and I'm going to ask you whether or not it changes your opinion about when you believe his mental capacity was significantly reduced. He was asked the following question: "Okay. What I'm interesting now is at the time of the incident by the river," that's the killing of the five men by the river, "was your mental state -- were you having any kind of mental problems or psychiatric problems at that time?" Mr. Vasiljevic's answer was: "No. I had problems after that incident, especially since a colleague of mine was killed there. So I felt bad. I felt sorry for what had happened, and I started developing a problem in the back of my head." That was his answer to his own assessment of his mental condition at the time that those five men were killed. Knowing that now, does that change in any way your opinion regarding when his capacity became severely reduced -- significantly reduced?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't change it, because I have to say that I speak on behalf of the information I received. These are authentic -- this is authentic information that I received based on my interview with Mr. Vasiljevic. But perhaps I have an explanation for what you quoted. My experience and our clinical experience says that we do not receive all of the information from our patients at the same time. Sometimes it happens that we see our patients that we follow regularly who all of a sudden subsequently start telling us about some of their problems that they had three years ago, five years ago, sometime in the past. What is a big question for me as a professional is what and how it happened that Mr. Vasiljevic gave me all of this information pertaining to heredity factors through his mother. I don't know whether it was a moment when we psychologists say he was in regression, a deep regression, and had a need to give this information to me. I couldn't tell you. I just know that this information was provided to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Doctor, you are being asked to consider that evidence now. That is what he said. He may not have said it to you, but you are being asked to consider that piece of information now. Does it change the view that you have expressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it doesn't change.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In the case history of the accused which you had and reviewed in preparation of your report, a doctor at Uzice hospital said the following: "The patient shows signs of a pre-delirium state." Can you describe or tell us what the doctor meant when the doctor wrote "shows signs of a pre-delirium state," if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have to say that this information that exists in his anamnesis was given by a colleague of mine. I don't know if it was a general practitioner or an orthopaedist who worked at the orthopaedic ward. So this is information that didn't come from a psychiatrist. What I believe to be important is that we cannot ignore alcoholism as a factor in development of his psychosis and whether this was a pre-delirium. I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Doctor, could you just tell us what are the symptoms of a pre-delirium state? What would be the observable symptoms?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the visible symptoms prior to delirium is a psychomotor anxiety, lack of sleep, an abundance of somatic symptoms, and perhaps an appearance of deceptive hallucinations. When we talk about delirium, usually those hallucinations are optical ones. Now, whether he showed these symptoms, I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And in your professional opinion, how soon after an alcoholic stops drinking do we first see the signs of a pre-delirium state?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- when a person stops drinking, it can produce two reactions. The first reaction can be an abstinence symptom and the second one could be a delirium. Now which one will emerge, we don't know. Mr. Vasiljevic had a trauma, and we should not disregard it, because he was suffering great pain, and delirium could have -- this could have contributed to his delirium. And this can develop 24 hours, 48 hours after a person stops drinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How much time would transpire, in your experience, between the initial onset or observation of this pre-delirium state and the actual onset of delirium tremens?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This can develop within a few hours or 24 hours. What is significant here, and I think that I need to stress this because I received this information from Mr. Vasiljevic during our interview in Detention Unit, is that he started experiencing, and I think it's very important, in the toxic stage of drinking that a person develops an addiction to alcohol and this person needs to consume alcohol. He told me that he was able, within a few days after admission, to obtain certain amounts of alcohol. Of course, we are talking about small amounts of alcohol here, but he was able to obtain it, which means that, while hospitalised, he was still able to obtain alcohol.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Doctor, before I leave the medical records or the case history, you testified, in response to a question by Mr. Domazet, that you had no information before you that Mr. Vasiljevic had ever been aggressive. Isn't it a fact that in the case history itself, there are at least one if not more reports by medical staff saying that Mr. Vasiljevic had engaged in aggressive behaviour?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That information is contained in a medical history, the last, the third medical history, given to us, but it says that he showed a psychomotor agitation. However, he wasn't aware of it. He wasn't aware of this condition. This wasn't under the control of his consciousness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I want to move to a different subject now. Yesterday, when you described some of the methods that you employed to come to your conclusion, you talked about trying to get documentation. Now, with respect to the death certificate of Mrs. Vasiljevic, Mr. Vasiljevic's mother, you stated, "I asked an attorney from Visegrad to get me the death certificate." Who was the attorney that you asked to get you this death certificate?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Rade Tanaskovic. He was the one to obtain this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And perhaps you're not the best person to answer this but you're the person who has had the document longer than any of us. I want to ask you a couple of questions regarding the document. In your experience, if somebody simply disappears and there is no recorded history that they had ever been treated for any mental illness, would a death certificate contain the assertion that they committed suicide and that they were mentally ill? And there is no evidence that any physical trace or any physical evidence of a suicide was found, just the fact that a person disappeared. In your experience, would a death certificate contain that information?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These type of death certificates have to be issued based on evidence and based of witness statements. This couldn't be issued just based on the fact that somebody came to the Court saying, "Well, this person has been missing for five years. We believe this person has committed suicide," and so on. There have to be witnesses who give statements based on which this disappearance is classified. This disappearance has been classified as suicide based on evidence produced that she had tried to commit suicide previously in the past. We have this as a data that was obtained through anamnesis, when Mr. Vasiljevic told me that his grandfather had already saved his mother once from the Drina River before. What we should not disregard either is that suicides are usually committed at dawn. We have an information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Doctor, please, you are not answering the question. The question doesn't ask you to put yourself in the place of the Court and whether you would have made those findings. The question is simply that in an ordinary death certificate, would you normally expect to have a reference to the fact that the death was caused by suicide? Is that your experience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That kind of information can be obtained. It could be noted in that document, that there was a suicide. However, this has to be based on witness statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Doctor, please don't try and force this upon us. The question is: Is this what you would usually find in a death certificate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Doctor, this document that you've given us here in Court, was it a public document or did you have to get some type of Court order to lift the seal or lift the privacy of this document?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you. This document was procured by the attorney, but I asked for this document because I know that these documents are normally issued. Now, what the procedure for their issuance is, is something that Mr. Tanaskovic can tell you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, doctor, again on this death certificate, although it appears that Mrs. Vasiljevic or Vojka Vasiljevic simply walked away on the 4th of July, 1963 and was never seen again, the day of her death was determined to be or fixed at the 16th of July, 1963. Is there any explanation given to you as to how somebody knew that she committed suicide on the 16th of July, if she had not been seen since the 4th of July?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, in Yugoslavia, if I am legally married to someone and I wish to marry somebody else, would I have to prove either that I was legally divorced from my wife or that my wife had died? Would I have to prove one of those two facts before I could legally marry a second time?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the legal procedure, yes. I couldn't tell you what the rules are for marriages concluded in church but as far as civil -- the institution of civil marriage is concerned, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The last paragraph of your report says the following, and I'd ask you to explain what exactly you mean by it: "The permanent duration of psychopathology in the first place, the drinking habit since 1973, surpasses the level of the reactive disorder and has permanent consequences of damaged personality." Can you briefly explain exactly what it is you mean by that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise but I only have a version in B/C/S so let me just take a look, please. You are talking about the English version. Which page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm assuming the English is just a translation of your original report in B/C/S, so please just look at the last paragraph of your original report.

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's on the last page, yes. What I had in mind when I said this, what I had in mind is the following, that alcoholism dating back to 1973 and the psychosis could not be a transient situation or a transient psychosis that had not left any -- [no interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We are getting no translation at all into English for this. Not since the words "transient psychosis that had not left any" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English booth now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just now, yes, just those last few words. Are you able to reproduce it or would you like the witness to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm sorry, the interpreters lost you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can try it. [Interpretation] I was saying it was not just the psychosis but drinking ever since 1973 led to certain organic changes. These are not of a reactive type. This cannot be viewed only within a certain fixed period of time during the psychosis, but they led to certain changes which are certainly quite evident in Mr. Vasiljevic's case, in the structure of his personality, and that is what we referred to yesterday, that psychological tests would be required to ascertain those changes, as well as an examination of his head by electrical procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And even if we were to conduct those tests and find damage, there would be no way of us telling when that damage or physical changes in his head first manifested or first occurred; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is something that would be significant for us. If we could -- we would be able to speak about a premorbid structure. Those tests would tell us the profile of the personality, and then if we had the specific tests indicating damage, then we would be able to make certain conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Doctor, yesterday, you testified - I just want to clarify what exactly you meant, and I'm quoting from the record: "If he is psychotic," and the record says, "I can," "he doesn't remember anything, and if he's not psychotic," again, "I can," "he does remember." Am I correct in believing that what you are saying is that the amount of memory he has and his ability to talk about and to recollect certain events that happened is an indication to you of whether or not he was psychotic?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just recollection. It is not the only indicator for psychotic condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm not saying it's the only one but is it one indicator?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is one of many, yes, one of, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now my next question to you is --

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But there are other indicators as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My next question to you is: Is this memory as an indicator, is it all or nothing or would a person's nearness to a psychotic state be evident by how good their recollection is? In other words, can a person have -- lie somewhere between no recollection and full recollection and will that also indicate to you the state of their mental health?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even the most psychotic patient can recollect some things, so we can't talk about this those categories, either/or. We can just say that for certain areas or certain periods in time, can there be clear recollection or gaps in memory or traces of recollection, but we can't simply put it either/or.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We will resume at 11.30. But Mr. Groome, it may be better, if I may suggest this to you, if you asked whether it affects his severe reduction in accountability rather than whether it affects his state of psychosis. They may not be exactly the same. The doctor has expressed herself differently at different times about that, and we are really concerned only about a reduced accountability.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Doctor, before the break we were talking about what conclusions you were able to draw from the quality of the accused's memory regarding certain events around this time, and the question I want to ask you is: Based on his recollection of the events, do you have an opinion regarding whether his capacity was significantly reduced when he began to talk about what happened on the 14th of June?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His capacity was reduced but not on the basis of disturbed recollection. His accountability was significantly reduced on the basis of certain other psychological conditions that he was in at the time. I cannot say that his recollections were disturbed in that period. He showed far more serious memory disturbance during the period of acute psychosis, that is, during his hospitalisation. Memories about the 14th of June are such that it is my impression that he is providing authentic information as to how the events took place, and if necessary, I can tell you what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Doctor, when you spoke about the standard in Yugoslavia, you said there were three standards. I want to talk about two of them. Can you differentiate for us the difference between reduced capacity and significantly reduced capacity?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When talking about capacity, we are talking about the intensity of fear felt by the person. That is one of the criteria affecting capacity. A second criterion affecting capacity is this feeling of fear as one psychological phenomenon, and another is will, somebody who has reduced will, who is suggestible. If his will is disturbed, that also affects capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Doctor --

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, the state of consciousness also affects capacity, but in this case, it is not measured because incapacity is -- is attributed to the state of consciousness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Doctor, how did you make the determination that Mr. Vasiljevic was not suffering from just a reduced capacity but of a significantly reduced capacity? What is the criteria you used and what are the observable symptoms that you found?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have already said, a feeling of fear, intensive fear that he felt in this period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm sorry to interrupt your answers, but I don't know whether you're listening to the question. What you are being asked is this: What are the criteria for differentiating between somebody who has a reduced capacity and somebody who has a significantly reduced capacity? Now, that doesn't relate to any particular matter to do with the accused in this case at the moment. You may be asked about that later. This is simply how do you determine that he was suffering from a reduced capacity or a significantly reduced capacity? What's the difference between the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of what we consider to be disturbances of affective conditions and conditions of will. Those are the two criteria. But how these are measured, that depends on the intensity and the quality of the symptoms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Doctor, if I understand you correctly, reduced and significantly reduced categories, you would expect the person to have some problem with fear and will, something that you could --

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] With affect, with affect. But in this situation it is fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: With affect regarding to fear --

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: -- and will.

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let's take fear first. Can you distinguish the difference between a person who has a problem with affect and fear that would be just reduced capacity and a person who would have significantly reduced capacity? What is the difference?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The intensity of fear. Mr. Vasiljevic said that he was constantly in fear. He was fearful for a long period that he refers to. In the case of significantly reduced capacity, this is constant fear. In the case of reduced capacity, it is not a continuous feeling of fear. In his case, he felt fear throughout and especially at night-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now let's talk about changes in affect regarding will. Can you give the same thing, give us an example of how you would distinguish between the two categories?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to will, the patient is suggestible. He is easily influenced. He is not capable of adopting a critical attitude towards a real-life event, and he cannot resist a situation he finds himself in. If he is also fearful, he cannot fully control himself and he may find himself in a situation when he has to defend himself from this subjective feeling of fear. In the situation he found himself in, he refused to carry out an order and allowed himself to be imprisoned. He could have even been court-martialled and executed. That could have happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you give us an example of somebody in the reduced category in this respect?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he had not been in this situation to be imprisoned, then he probably could have been in the category of reduced capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you're saying but for this imprisonment, you would entertain the possibility that regarding the affect and will, he would fit into the first category, simply reduced capacity?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And you are under the impression that his imprisonment could have resulted in a possible court-martial or an execution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with the laws, but I assume you can check in our legislation, and under conditions of war, if you do not execute an order, then you are subject to certain rules which envisage very strict sanctions. The punishment is much stricter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, aside from these two criteria, the affect regarding fear and the affect regarding will, are there any other categories or indicators that you look for in determining whether a person is -- has a reduced capacity or a significantly reduced capacity?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a category of a critical attitude towards reality. In a real-life situation, we must always know what we can expect or what might be a certain requirement of us. However, in this situation, we see that this critical attitude towards reality had changed. He didn't seem to perceive reality. He was guided by fear in his behaviour, rather than his consciousness or his awareness of his acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, doctor, you keep going back to fear, and it seems that it was a very important criteria, your belief that during this time period, he was suffering from a constant sense of fear; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, in this period, not now. At the time, yes, but now, no. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Back in 1992 --

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I explain why I don't think that applies now?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: We are not very concerned with today. Just 1992. I want to give you a fact that you are obviously unaware of and ask you does it change your opinion regarding whether he was in a constant state of fear. During the very time period that we are talking about, Mr. Vasiljevic turned in his weapon to his superiors and told them that he no longer needed it, even said, I believe, "What do I need it for? I'm just in the town." Does that change your opinion whether or not Mr. Vasiljevic was in a constant state of fear during the time period we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand what you said. He handed over his weapon to his superior why? Was there an explanation? Why did he hand in his weapon?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The explanation that Mr. Vasiljevic gave this Court, he said that he told his superior, "I do not need the weapon. What do I need it for? I am in the town. I'm in the town of Visegrad." Does that change your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. Why should it change my opinion? This could in fact confirm his uncritical attitude towards reality or that there was a fear, this subjective part, that may have existed at the time, and it was not objectively evident for people around him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, doctor, you've talked significantly or have spoken significantly regarding the impact of hereditary on mental disease, and we have also heard testimony that a niece of Mr. Vasiljevic's had a schizophrenic disorder, and we've heard about -- I think you've described him as having an affective disorder, and my question to you is: If a particular family is predisposed to schizophrenia, does that also mean that they are predisposed to affective disorders?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we are taught and what we teach our students is that the hereditary factor has more percentage-wise influence on affective orders than schizophrenia. As to whether in a family that has affective disorders, will lead to schizophrenia in distant relatives, we may assume that these may be connected but not necessarily so. The hereditary factor is far more dominant in relation to affective disorders. We don't know what the other ancestors of the young woman were like, whether it is just because on the maternal side there is this hereditary factor. Maybe there may be the same factor on the father's side but we don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Doctor, is there any study that you're aware of that would support a conclusion that the fact that his niece was schizophrenic indicates that he is predisposed towards a mental illness, affective disorder?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot directly link the niece and the mental health of Mr. Vasiljevic. What I am asserting here is that the direct link is through the mother. So we can talk about Mr. Vasiljevic's mother, who is the grandmother of this young woman. So her heredity factor comes from there. So that is the way it has been inherited, on the maternal side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question about Mr. Vasiljevic's mother. Yesterday you made the statement that his mother suffered from affective psychosis, and my question to you is: Based on the very limited information that we have regarding Mr. Vasiljevic's mother, how are you able to draw such a conclusive diagnosis regarding her mental condition?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reached my assumption and conclusion because I obtained information about the way she died, that is, suicide. Then I was told about attempted suicide a year and a half prior to her disappearance and suicide. The type of suicide is something that is an indicator of such a possible disease. Also the fact that she had changes of mood, an affect as a dominant symptom, and all this leads me to opt for affective psychosis. And that it is a psychosis, I need to emphasise once again, is confirmed by the moment when she disappeared. This is two months after childbirth, and this can most probably be considered as a puerperal psychosis, as we call it, that is, post-delivery psychosis. We locate them only in time but not in the contextual genetic sense. They are definitely endogenous psychoses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Doctor, would you agree with me that you are in some sense speculating regarding what Mrs. Vasiljevic may or may not have suffered from? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say I am speculating if I have 28 years of clinical experience when I have occasion to hear about such case histories and to read about them in our literature. So this is quite a typical example of depression and how puerperal psychosis is diagnosed and psychosis in that period of life. This is something that I studied and that I teach my students.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Doctor, of the family history that we've heard regarding the Vasiljevics, all of the mental illness, aside from Mr. Vasiljevic, has been in the women in the family, and based on your experience and any studies that you have read, is this predisposition towards mental illness, is it affected by the sex of the person?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, doctor, a Prosecution psychiatrist also examined Mr. Vasiljevic. Can I ask you, did you have an opportunity to see her report?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And did you read her report?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about her conclusions and -- do you agree with her conclusions, and if you do not, could you please tell us where you differ in opinion?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree in my colleague's Vera Folnegovic-Smalc's conclusion which in great detail expressed her opinion as regards the period of hospitalisation and possible diagnosis for that period that she speculates about, and I think that our finding in that respect is very similar. She also speaks about the hereditary factor, about the fact of alcoholism, commenting on the possible diagnostic categories. She speaks about the psychosis as a diagnosis. And what is also something that I underlined as well, that this cannot be observed only from the biological standpoint or only from the standpoint of alcoholism or only from the stress factor but that these are interdependent conditions. And regardless of the etiological factor that we will opt for, whether it is alcohol or psychosis, it is quite evident that in that period he manifested this kind of behaviour. And in that sense, I fully agree with her finding, and I think that our opinions are very close. What I do not see in her report is reference to the period prior to the psychosis. There is no comment as to the evaluation of the mental condition of Mr. Vasiljevic in the period prior to hospitalisation and prior to the psychosis. I think that this should be included.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In her report, she describes or compares the Yugoslavian diagnosis with DSM-IV and with the definition provided by the World Health Organisation. Are you in agreement with her that the diagnosis of his condition back in 1992 regarding the DSM-IV, the substance-withdrawal delirium, and with respect to the World Health Organisation, withdrawal syndrome with delirium? Would you agree that that is most probably what Mr. Vasiljevic suffered from at the time of his hospitalisation?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I interpreted the finding of Professor Folnegovic as her differential diagnostic thinking, and in that sense I agree with her. But she did not opt specifically for one of those diagnoses because it is absolutely impossible to opt for one single diagnosis because none of those diagnoses -- that the criteria for one of those diagnoses have not been fulfilled, because we have symptoms which would speak for delirium and others for psychosis, which only shows that this was a psychosis provoked by multiple factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let me be more specific. Let's take the DSM-IV definition of substance withdrawal delirium. Would you agree of the symptoms described in that definition that Mr. Vasiljevic possessed those symptoms?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Which ones do you say that he did not possess?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had them, but he had some others. He had a surplus of symptoms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So it is based on your finding that -- or your belief that he had additional symptoms that makes you diagnose him differently?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were to have to opt for a particular diagnosis, then I would choose the diagnosis of psychosis. It is ICD-10, F1X5, which describes a psychotic disorder which is linked also to alcoholism.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, doctor, yesterday you, in response to a question by Mr. Domazet, Mr. Domazet had asked you could the stress that triggers this lapse into mental disease, could it be standing and watching some people be murdered and possibly even one of -- and possibly even knowing one of the people that was murdered, and you said yes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, aside from an event like that, let me ask you -- it may seem like an obvious question, but would you agree that it would also be possible that the triggering event could be standing and watching approximately 80 people put into a house and the house set on fire, that that kind of -- witnessing that type of event would also be sufficiently stressful to trigger a lapse into mental disease; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that when I said yesterday that this was one of the factors, I wish to emphasise that never for a moment am I talking about a single factor but only multiple factors. So we have to view those factors in a dynamic relationship. But as one of the stress factors, certainly, yes, the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And you've made that clear in your testimony. I believe what you were talking about yesterday was - I don't know how this expression will translate, but the event that -- the straw that breaks the camel's back, the final event that pushes the person over the edge and we can then begin to see observable psychiatric symptoms. That is the context that you were talking about this yesterday. So my question to you is: Could witnessing the mass murder of approximately 80 people, would you agree with me that that is a sufficiently stressful event that could trigger this lapse into mental disease that you've described?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you because I did not get any such information. I spoke only about the information I obtained, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Doctor --

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I was not told about any such event, so I don't know what effect it would have had on Mr. Vasiljevic if it had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm asking you a hypothetical question, not about Mr. Vasiljevic at this time. Would you agree with me that witnessing that type of crime would be sufficiently stressful to act as the type of trigger that you told us about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the structure of the personality. If he is a hypersensitive personality, yes, but we don't know the structure of the personality in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I think that the question you asked was an unfortunate one because it allows the doctor to go off on this sort of a trail. Why don't you ask her, as a truly hypothetical question but about Mr. Vasiljevic, would witnessing the fire in which 80 people died be sufficient to have set him off? That's what you're really after, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You've heard the Judge's question. Would you answer that, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a stress which can trigger such a disease, but it can only contribute to the outbreak of the disease but it cannot cause it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, again I want to ask you a hypothetical question regarding Mr. Vasiljevic and to ask you your opinion. That same event, could it not also serve as a trigger if, for whatever reason, Mr. Vasiljevic participated in that crime in some manner? Could that -- could having participated in such a crime not also be a triggering event?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a direct answer to that question, we have to have a profile of the personality structure. For such a direct answer, we have to know the defence mechanisms that the patient has.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Doctor, let's confine ourselves to Mr. Vasiljevic. You've testified that witnessing -- Mr. Vasiljevic's witnessing of such an event could trigger him. My question to you is: Could Mr. Vasiljevic's participation in the event also trigger the mental disease that you've described?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer such questions directly when Mr. Vasiljevic is named because in the interview I had with him, I was not given any information that could tell me what the -- his reaction would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Doctor, this is the third time that you've gone off on that particular trail. You are being asked now to consider it. Whether you were told by Mr. Vasiljevic or not, you are being asked whether his participation in that fire would have been sufficient to have set him off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All we could talk about is the stress factor. Now, whether it would affect him or not and how, I cannot tell you, as I don't have the psychological profile of his personality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So, doctor, you are able to tell us that merely witnessing -- Mr. Vasiljevic witnessing the event could be the trigger but you're not able to tell us whether his participation in it could be the trigger. Is that what your testimony is now?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that now. I couldn't tell you because it depends -- it would depend on how he would feel had he participated and that is also linked to the structure of the personality, and we also don't know whether he would allow himself to participate in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Doctor, your findings rely significantly on information provided by Mr. Vasiljevic, information regarding blinking, magical thinking, his thoughts about the importance or the relevance of crows versus doves, his belief that he could subconsciously communicate with his wife, his belief in some prohibition from God, the suicide of his mother. All of these facts, none of your colleagues who treated him in 1992 were aware of, who treated him in the psychiatric ward of Uzice hospital. They had no recollection of him ever telling them those things, nor in reviewing the medical records, they saw no notes regarding any of these things. Can you entertain the possibility, however slight you may believe it to be, that Mr. Vasiljevic could be trying to avoid responsibility for crimes he committed by fabricating some of these symptoms and some of these facts? Can you entertain that possibility in any way?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that the level of education of Mr. Vasiljevic does not give us the right to assume something like that, because what I learned from the interview is something that fits into the clinical picture of what we can see now and what we could see in the past, so the only remaining question is why did he start talking about his symptoms this late? This is something that I mentioned just recently, that occasionally, some of our patients will give us their symptoms or talk about their symptoms after the passage of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Doctor --

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't doubt that these symptoms exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that this was invented.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you entertain the possibility that some of the facts and some of the symptoms that he described for you may possibly be fabricated? Can you entertain that possibility?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Doctor, I want to ask you a few questions only to try and clear up my understanding of your evidence. I'm not challenging you in any way, but I have had some difficulty in following the logic of some of your evidence. You told us that one of the triggers to this particular mental state was the fear which Mr. Vasiljevic had during the course of the war. And you drew our attention to what he himself has said, that he was fearful at one stage when he was required to deliver food in dangerous areas. And that he was so fearful of that that he refused to do it and that's what landed him in prison. Now, once that fear that he says he had at that time, or once the cause of that fear that he said he had at the time, has been removed, does this particular psychosis or reduced, significantly reduced, responsibility continue? And if so, for how long?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The state of fear is a state that a person goes through unconsciously. If a person could control fear, then a person could remove it. So this was provoked by the front line and by the tasks that he was given and could not discharge, which is why he ended up in prison. So it doesn't mean that once we remove the cause, the fear would disappear automatically. It still remained with him, and these symptoms that kept developing are a further proof of the fact the fear remained, this blinking, his thoughts, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You see, after he came out of prison, he wasn't sent back to anywhere near the front line. He was given this task of cleaning up the town or supervising the citizens in cleaning up the town. And whilst nobody would suggest that this particular town was free of any trouble, it was nothing like a front line. How long would this psychosis or this significantly reduced accountability continue after the cause of his fear had been removed?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
