utterances.text: What I obtained, the information that I obtained, is that upon arriving, coming into town, so once he started cleaning, he started drinking even more, so this other factor that is constantly present was still there, even to a greater degree. He said that he went into town to -- and visited houses where he was sure he would be offered a drink. And this simply contributed to deteriorating his state. It was not improving it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You also told us that had he not been sent to prison, his condition would only have been one of reduced capacity rather than significantly reduced capacity. So that obviously the fact that he went to prison had some effect upon his mental state; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not understand each other well, then. What I said is that had he not been sent to prison, had he not been -- had he not put himself in the situation to be sent to prison, then we could describe that condition as a condition of reduced accountability, but his behaviour was already such that he was non-critical, and this is why he in the end went to prison. So the prison is just a form but not the substance of the matter. The substance is his non-critical attitude with respect to tasks that were assigned to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that's certainly saying it a lot more clearly, if I may say so, than you said it before. So that once he is removed from being in prison, you say that would have had no effect in reducing the state of his unaccountability or increasing his accountability, I suppose is the best way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't change significantly the level of his accountability because he continued drinking and continued acting in a non-critical way, an irresponsible way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you want to ask any questions, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Further examination by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Lopicic, as regards this period of time that we have just discussed, which is the time spent in prison that you seem to view as the time when Mitar Vasiljevic's accountability was significantly reduced, the questions you have just answered pertain to the period immediately after that. So this is what I would like to focus on right now. In addition to what you have just stated, could the fact that precisely after leaving the prison, based on his testimony and other testimony here, he attended the funeral of his cousin that same week, five or six days later. Unfortunately, we don't know on what day he was exactly in prison and released, in addition to what took place a day or two later, which is linked to what he described as the execution of people on the Drina.

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are the stressful moments that I described. I would simply like to highlight that this departure, release from prison, if I understood Mr. Vasiljevic correctly when he described this to me, is one of the reasons why he -- one of the reasons why he was released from the prison was the very fact that he was told that a very close relative of his had been killed, so he needed to go to the funeral. I have to say that there is a special affective link between Mr. Vasiljevic and his uncle, and this -- he's been speaking of this uncle from the very first day as a person who took good care of children after the mother's disappearance. And another fact that evidences this is that there is a physical similarity between the two of them and that people would frequently confuse them in Visegrad when his uncle was younger. So he was especially close to this uncle of his. The uncle had an only son, so Mr. Vasiljevic was certainly affected by the death of this only son of the uncle to whom he was very close. This uncle was the mother's brother. If we can add, this event of the 7th is this very stressful -- is the fact that among those who were executed was his colleague and his son, and he had a very good professional relationship with this colleague of his and this certainly affected him to a great deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I would like to ask you something pertaining to the 14th of July -- June, which he also discussed. And bearing in mind that you spoke about the quantity of memory as one of the factors, the fact that on the 14th of June he drank at Pionirska Street with Mujo Halilovic and that he remembered this and that almost everything described by witnesses he could not remember, and some of the witnesses spoke of him having told them that he was in charge of refugees, that he allegedly worked for the Red Cross, that he even gave some kind of a written statement, certificate claiming that he did not remember this. So he does not remember any of the things that took place on the 14th of June except for this event when he went to get the horse.

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. I don't know how much alcohol he drank on that day. What I was told is he had one bottle of brandy that he started drinking that very morning, and if I remember correctly, in my report it says here that he gave Mujo the remainder of that bottle and then they went to get the horse. So there are some state of acute drunkenness when a person cannot remember a certain event. Now, whether he was in that particular state of acute drunkenness I cannot assert because I have no facts that would pertain to this. But I was given the information that I have pertained to that moment when he had been injured. If he drank more, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Both of you, please remember to pause. You're both coming in on top of the interpreter. So, Doctor --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- just wait until the question is finished and then pause before you begin your answer. And, Mr. Domazet, you have slipped. You have been very good, but that was very early.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked you this in context of what you replied when asked by Judge Hunt whether after that period, around June 1st and until June 14th, whether his state improved during that time or not. Now, whether these circumstances; namely, that he does not remember events described by witnesses, providing that the witnesses are telling the truth as well, whether this would influence the reduction of his accountability or not.

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, this further confirms this claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So the fact that he took the horse, after what we just described, and he rode the horse according to what he himself stated, as did the witnesses, without saddle, without any kind of equipment, so he rode the horse without shoes through the town on asphalt roads, and according to some witnesses he was going quite fast, would this contribute to this kind of behaviour of his?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that this is to some extent a non-critical attitude acting. We know what can happen if one is riding a horse without shoes, horseshoes, on the asphalt road, et cetera. There's no gripping there. So obviously this is not appropriate. And this further confirms what we've been saying, that he at that time had a non-critical or modified attitude with respect to reality, but not to the degree where we could call this psychotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this pertains to this period, and if you were to say -- to discuss this period of significantly reduced accountability, and in May of 1992, this period that you also at some point described as a period containing one of these indicators, the fear. Now, would it be possible that he had this similar condition during this period or even a more intense condition or you have no facts to base this on?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said is that during this interview, I obtained information on fears that he had during that time at the end of May, but he didn't mention all of these symptoms as being linked to that period. Some of them he mentioned as being linked to a period later than that. So I don't have sufficient information for that period, but it was end of May when he started developing these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now, when we're talking about what Mr. Groome brought up, when Mr. Vasiljevic returned a weapon, based on Mr. Groome's question, Mr. Vasiljevic returned this weapon and said, "I don't need this in Visegrad any more." I think this transpired in a somewhat different way; namely, that he returned the weapon because he did not want to go to the front line. So he refused to be sent to the front line, which is a much more serious set of circumstances than the situation described by Mr. Groome when he allegedly said, "I don't need this any more." So I think this to be the real reason behind this. And would this change anything in your reply?

utterances.speaker: ZORKA LOPICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this could only be a sign of his fear or once again a sign of his non-critical attitude. I did not receive the information about him returning the weapon, so I can't tell you anything further.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You've already replied to this, but I simply thought perhaps you had some more information regarding this. Thank you. I don't have any further questions. I think that all of these questions arose based on the questions of Mr. Groome. So that's all I had. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, thank you, doctor, for coming along to give evidence and for the evidence which you gave. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Domazet, I have -- I understand that you have told the Trial Chamber's legal officer that Dr. Stojkovic is not coming; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So this is the end of your case then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'm finished with the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you've got dates here for the 11th, which is tomorrow, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have the two experts arriving tomorrow as per our previous arrangement with the Chamber. One is flying in tonight, and the other has a teaching commitment today and he was the professor who was here for a day and a half before the break, but he will be here first thing tomorrow morning. So what the Prosecution is proposing is the two experts tomorrow and then the remainder of the Prosecution rejoinder case on Monday morning. I expect that the Prosecution case will be completed by Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Even the psychiatrist?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Maybe I'm too optimistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't know what experience you have of taking psychiatrists their through evidence, but it is difficult to keep them within any reasonable bounds, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We will certainly do our best to finish on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There was -- the Prosecution was going to call Investigator Roy to admit two documents which are now relevant in rejoinder. Mr. Domazet has agreed to their admissibility so there is no need to call him. I have the documents here and marked. If it's convenient to the court, I'll pass them up now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: They are Prosecution documents, two packages. One is 171 and one is -- sorry, 170 and the other is 171.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The package of 170 is the correspondence regarding medical records of Uzice hospital, correspondence between the Office of the Prosecutor and the government of Republika Srpska as an intermediary with the hospital. The Prosecution document package 171 is a similar request to the Republika Srpska regarding the existence of any complaints made against Milan Lukic or Sredoje Lukic during the time period concerning in this case, and their response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's going in as part of your case in reply, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Is there any objection to that, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I have no objection to this being admitted, but I truly regret that I have not seen any of these exhibits previously, especially those pertaining to Uzice. One of them was signed by a witness who came to testify here, in which case we would have had questions for that witness, but unfortunately this has -- was only brought to our attention now, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, so the transcript is clear, these documents were provided yesterday and I asked Mr. Domazet to review them and let me know this morning whether he'd agreed to their admissibility, which is what was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But I'm just a little concerned as to the point that Mr. Domazet has raised. Which particular document is it that has been signed by a witness that you would have asked some questions on?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I saw a document here, a reply from the health centre in Uzice to the municipal court in Uzice, of 17th April, 2001, and it was signed by Dr. Aleksandar Moljevic. Although based on previously exchanged letters, one can see that they were sent to the director of the hospital, and Dr. Moljevic is not even a head of the orthopaedic ward. He gave a reply which pertains to the undisputable confiscation of documentation held by him, on the 1st of November, 2000. However, he did not say, or this document does not say whether there are any other relevant documents which could be used here and which would explain why such a reply was given. I know that as a Defence counsel, I encountered a serious problem concerning the lack of access to the documents in the Uzice hospital after the 1st of November, 2000 because they believed that the originals of these documents were confiscated or seized from them, and up until the beginning of this trial. The situation was somewhat improved due to some write-ups in the papers, confirming that Mr. Vasiljevic was in Visegrad after the 14th of June, based on which a number of physicians called and expressed willingness to come and testify. And I am really sorry that this couldn't have been done earlier, and had we known of the existence of these letters, perhaps we could have done something earlier as well. But otherwise, I have no objection to these being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But Mr. Domazet, my concern is your complaint that you would have asked this doctor some questions about this letter if you had known that the letter was going to be tendered or that you knew that it existed. My understanding is that you were there present when the documents were seized from the doctor, were you not? So you knew they'd been seized. You knew the doctor was being called. What is there in this letter, other than a misspelling of my name, that you could have asked him about, that you haven't had the opportunity to ask the doctor about in any event?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Maybe there is a misunderstanding. It has nothing to do with the 1st of November, 2000. That is, everything is in order. What I consider is not in order is the answer that all the documents were seized on that occasion, because we saw that there were relevant documents in the hospital which were brought by witnesses here in court much later, and that is why I would have had some questions, not with regard to the actual seizure, which I attended, and which was carried out in a perfectly official manner, and I have nothing to say about that. It was based on an order that existed at the time. But there was some talk about Dr. Moljevic refusing to sign because apparently he was promised that he could take back the originals and leave the photocopies, but that's a problem between Mr. Moljevic and officials of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I remember the doctor's evidence that he was considerably embarrassed by the fact that they had been seized, and when he gave that evidence, he was looking directly at me, I remember. But that's a different matter. I'm still concerned to know what is the problem about this document going into evidence. He says all documents on Mitar Vasiljevic's case were seized. I think what he is saying is simply all the documents he had were seized. I don't read that letter as any assertion by him that all of the documents that the hospital had relating to your client were seized on that occasion, just the ones he had with him. They were the only ones that were seized. Now, if that's the way we interpret the letter, which I don't think is of any particular consequence one way or the other, are you concerned about this letter going into evidence? May I say this to you in addition? You have, as you have pointed out, had access now to a lot of other letters and documents that dealt with your client. Now, have you been in any way prejudiced by your lack of knowledge of the existence of that letter? I notice that the doctor's name is misspelled as well, but that letter of the 17th of April? That doesn't go to its admissibility, I should hasten to add, but have you had some problem in the conduct of your case? I myself can't see it, but if you can point something out to me, I would be very interested to know what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, absolutely no. There is no problem, absolutely not. I just said that I was sorry that I didn't know of this letter, and that Dr. Moljevic didn't tell us about it either, because then I would have had some questions for him in this connection, but it is not all that important for us to need to hear anyone in this connection, including Dr. Moljevic. If the Prosecution received this belatedly, that's another matter. I thought they had it earlier on, and I thought it was a pity that we didn't have access to these documents when the doctors from Uzice came here. But certainly I don't think that it is of great relevance, and I have no objection to them being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, they will be Exhibits P170 and P171. Still, I have to say this, though: I still do not understand how you have been prejudiced in any way by not knowing of the existence of that letter until after the doctor had given evidence, because he could not have given you anything more than what he has said, that all of the documents he had with him were seized, as you knew because you were there. All right. That, then, is as far as --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but, Your Honour, all the documents that the witness brought with him were seized, all the documents that he brought to Visegrad, but we know that certain witnesses brought other documents that were later admitted into evidence which he didn't bring at the time, and it would have been a good thing if he had said that there were other documents in which Mitar Vasiljevic is mentioned, but this wasn't done. I don't think that I was prejudiced as a result, as those documents have been admitted, but Your Honour, I would like to take advantage of this opportunity maybe now, with respect to -- to say something about future documents tendered by the Prosecution. I'm referring to the expert witnesses that have been planned on the basis of a list that I have received, and I have nothing to say in that connection. I am worried about two witnesses who have been proposed for next week by the Prosecution. I received yesterday, for the second witness, whose name I will not mention, I can just give you the initials, because I'm not sure whether the Prosecution will require protective measures for him, it is a witness who appears for the first time, and judging by what I have received, which is not a statement but rather a summary as to what the witness told the investigators about, I think it cannot be the rebuttal case of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is it the witness with the initials BB?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, I see. Well, you're challenging that as a matter in reply or rebuttal? I just want to see what the point is that you're making.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because according to the Rules of Procedure, the Prosecution may call new witnesses in the rebuttal stage but for very specific situations. I do not see that what this witness told investigators about is something that could serve as reply of the Prosecution to the Defence case, and I fear that the testimony of this witness about quite different circumstances that we have not gone into would lead to me having to try and find rebuttal evidence against it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then, what you are saying is that you challenge that as appropriate evidence to be called at this stage of the case, and if that's so, then I'll hear what Mr. Groome has got to say about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, in substance, the witness will testify, and I haven't spoken to the witness, but it's on the 21st or 22nd of June, the witness, with about a hundred other people, were gathered in the Karadzic school, and at the time Mr. Vasiljevic and Mr. Lukic walked into that school. Mr. Vasiljevic set up at a table with a logbook and said that, "I'm working for the Red Cross and I have to list all your names which I will then forward to Geneva and then you'll be sent to a host country." He's not alleging he committed any other crime other than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This is an issue as to whether or not he could have been in hospital, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, it's also, Your Honour -- in the Defence case now, we've heard from several witness who have denied, even though they had previous statements saying that he wore the mark of the Red Cross, that he had never represented himself as a Red Cross member, and they denied that in Court that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. But, Mr. Groome, that is an issue that you set out to prove in your case in chief, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was testimony in the Prosecution case that at the time of the crime, Mr. Vasiljevic represented himself as a member of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Some -- from Red Cross. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The only evidence that that was not true or that he had not represented himself came in on the Defence case, the several witnesses who said that at no time did they ever see him wearing a Red Cross emblem, even though in their previous case the information that I had was that they would be testifying here that they -- he had worn the emblem of the Red Cross on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: One witness had in his statement that it was a cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe it was three witnesses, Your Honour, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: One of them precisely said a red cross. The other ones were at least consistent with it. And you've got all of that out in evidence. But it was an issue which you sought to litigate in your case in chief. So -- and this person, BB, let's call him, could have been called in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- I'm not sure that's correct, Your Honour, in that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, yes, he could. Oh, yes, he could. You set out to prove that Mr. Vasiljevic turned up that afternoon sometime and was representing himself as somebody from the Red Cross and directing them into the first of the houses that they were put in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That was your case. You opened it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. If I can ask what relevance would it have been that at a time later, over a week later when we're not alleging any crime was committed, that he set himself up in an auditorium and gathered these people together to say, "I'm with the Red Cross; let me get your names." I don't see how that would have been relevant to the issue of what happened on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It was put to him in the course of the original interview that he was wearing a Red Cross thing, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That he was wearing? No. Just he -- he, in his interview, said he wore a red ribbon. That was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Was he not asked about the Red Cross in that interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He was asked if he said that he was a member of the Red Cross to the people, did he tell them to go into the house. He denied that he said anything to these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's right. So that he would -- you would have been entitled to show that he had on another occasion represented himself as being from the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I guess my understanding of what I would have been entitled to do, which is what the Prosecution did do, is to show that on the 14th, when he said he didn't make any of those representations, is to call evidence that on the 14th he did that. I don't think I would have been entitled to call the one or the several or the hundred people in the Karadzic school a week later who saw him taking names on behalf of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It would have been just as relevant then as it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would respectfully disagree with the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I can't see this as a case in reply. You are seeking to contradict his denial by proof that subsequently he did represent himself elsewhere as the -- as being from the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And that was a denial that you had from the word go.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm seeking to contradict what I tried to bring out with Defence witnesses, their statements that he had worn the Red Cross symbol. All that he denied -- he made a blanket denial of everything that -- that witnesses had -- what he -- when the interview was taken, he was -- "Informed witnesses say that you did these -- you said four things." He made a blanket denial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So that was an issue from the very beginning of the case, that he was denying that he had ever represented himself as being from the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it doesn't matter on that day or else. If you want to prove that he did represent himself as being from the Red Cross on that day by proof that he had done it some weeks later now, that's what you're trying to do now, you could have done it in your case in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, if the Court is going to rule against this as being appropriate rebuttal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to find out how it is a matter in reply. We are not ruling on anything. But the challenge has been made, and I frankly cannot see how it is in reply. You are seeking to bolster the case that you set out to prove in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've made the Prosecution's position clear or as clear as I can make it. If the Court disagrees with the Prosecution's position, I would then move to reopen the Prosecution's direct case to allow this witness to testify regarding a very important fact in his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then you have to explain why it is that you didn't call him in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It was my misunderstanding of what was appropriate in the case in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ah, Mr. Groome, innocence by counsel is an excuse that is often put forward but not often accepted. You're an experienced counsel. If you think that it is relevant now, then you could have thought that it was relevant then. It's the same relevance to the same issue, his denial that he had represented himself as being from the Red Cross. And if it was relevant -- if it's relevant now, it was relevant then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the Pre-Trial Conference, the Court urged the Prosecution to limit our witnesses to the bare minimum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. I also said very clearly at some stage, either the Pre-trial or at one of the Status Conferences, that this rather lax attitude that some Trial Chambers used to have about allowing parties to have cases in reply, rebuttal, rejoinder, et cetera, was not going to be permitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, however mistaken I may have been, that witness was not put into the Prosecution direct case because the Prosecution believed that this witness's testimony about something that happened in this school at a time not associated with the crime would not have been considered appropriate in the Prosecution's evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE  HUNT
utterances.text: Is there anything more you want to put?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On this issue, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you want to say anything in reply, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to reply that in the materials I received prior to trial, there were quite a number of witness statements that referred to certain events in the fire brigade centre or somewhere else around the 20th of June or later, and those witnesses were not called for the case in chief, nor were they examined though their statements were known. So I was surprised to see this witness appearing to testify about these circumstances which could provoke some other evidence, because what the Defence has learnt inquiring about people who did work in the Red Cross, we came across a person who physically resembles the accused, who worked in the Red Cross at the time and who may have been in this situation that the witness refers to. But this was evidence that I didn't think we should call because it was not called by the Prosecution. So that I fear that the introduction of this kind of evidence would indeed trigger fresh evidence from us, because if we were to talk about a Red Cross official at the time who took down the names of those people in the school on the 22nd of June, and if it was claimed that that was Mitar Vasiljevic, I would have to provide evidence to prove that it was quite another person. As for this other witness statement, and I had his statement before trial, is he being called for the same circumstances or only for the recording of the tape on which we have already heard a witness? And my understanding is that witnesses will be called who were present when the tape was recorded, which is in dispute here. So if that is what this other witness is to testify about, that is permissible. But if he's being called to testify about something else, since this witness's statement exists and it was disclosed to me by the Prosecution, then in that case, I think it would not be appropriate to examine this witness about any other events either except for those that have already been raised in the proceedings so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You're referring there to VG97, are you? The one who is going to give evidence about a conversation with Mr. Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That particular matter, as we've already ruled, is in reply, but that doesn't mean that the Prosecution can ask him anything else. They can call evidence which is properly evidence in reply. If you go in and ask some questions in cross-examination, of course, that may open up all sorts of issues, that the Prosecution can only call evidence from that witness which is in reply, which is the making of the tape or the conversation which it is alleged Mr. Savic had during the course of what one of the Defence witnesses calls the cocktail party.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You are not limited in your cross-examination, but anything you open up in cross-examination enables the Prosecution to deal with it. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, all of that discussion regarding what you've just talked about on the record has been in private session just to protect that issue regarding that witness. Perhaps just in caution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's not in private session at all. What are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: About what Mr. Savic -- the tape recording, Mr. Savic. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We only referred to them by the pseudonym VG97. That's a different matter. I don't think there's any real problem about that. But, Mr. Groome, that does raise, however, or remind me of an issue that I thought first of all. The fact that you are going to call BB, that something happened on the 22nd of June, that was something which was clearly in issue in the case, that he was not in hospital on the 22nd of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And the Prosecution made a selection of witnesses prior to trial and chose not to choose this witness because this witness was somewhat reluctant and because of where the witness lived. I will not be calling the witness for that but only for the matter regarding the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But it will inevitably get into evidence the fact that Mr. Vasiljevic was not in hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, I'm certain -- Your Honour, that could be cured by limiting what the Court uses as evidence. The Court -- I mean, I would certainly agree to the Court just using the fact that he signed the -- he represented himself and took the -- took the names as being the only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And represented himself from being from the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Right. And then saying he would send the names off to Geneva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, we'll have to discuss that matter, and we'll let you know. We will attempt to give you a decision either late this afternoon or by tomorrow morning. So we start off tomorrow then with the two -- Ton Broeders from the forensic institute. Is that about documents or about what?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He is the person who analysed the voice on the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before we -- on the other matter, the witness is scheduled to take the plane tomorrow morning, so the Prosecution would certainly appreciate if there was word this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Very well, then. We will let you know if we can. So that's all we can do today. We'll adjourn now until 9.30 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one simple matter. The Prosecution originally had the two linguists, the one who spoke B/C/S that assisted in the analysis. After a consultation with Mr. Domazet, there's an agreement, or Mr. Domazet agrees that there is nothing he wishes to ask on cross-examination, so the Prosecution will not be calling that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is the statement in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It makes up part of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And that report is not yet in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No. It will come in through Dr. Broeders, and the first witness tomorrow morning will be Dr. Raby. He has a plane to catch in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What about the doctor from Gouda, Mr. Domazet? You wanted to ask him some -- you wanted to get his report into evidence - in fact, it's in evidence - but you had to produce him for cross-examination. I forget the doctor's name but he comes from something called Green Heart at Gouda, spelled G-O-U-D-A.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have decided not to call this witness. It would probably complicate things, the whole case, now that we are near the end, for me to call him now. I have not had any contact with that doctor, as he was called by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But he wasn't called by the Prosecution. The Prosecution obtained the report and disclosed it to you under Rule 68. You have tendered it and it was in evidence upon the basis you would produce him for cross-examination. Now, if you don't want to produce him for cross-examination, then the report must be withdrawn from evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm aware of that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: As long as you're aware of that. Which number was it so that we can note that it's been withdrawn? D41. Exhibit D41 has been withdrawn. All right. We'll resume at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
